speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. SPEAKER    STATEMENT RESPECTING MOTION BY MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext:
May I refer to the question of privilege raised in the house yesterday by the Minister of Justice. In the July 15 issue of Hansard at page 2167 the Minister of Justice is reported as having raised a question of privilege in the following words:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On Friday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) rose on a question of privilege, as reported at page 2121 of Hansard, which I think I can summarize. I quote:
"My point of privilege is that what we now have is precisely what we had last June. We have the government construing that the Financial Administration Act or regulations made under it gives them authority to do something which the act itself says cannot be done. The Financial Administration Act says that no appointments by the treasury board can be made under it."
The Minister of Justice then went on to say:
The hon. member's statement in this respect is not correct. If hon. members would look at section 5 (2) of the Financial Administration Act they would find it provides that the governor in council may authorize the treasury board to exercise all or any of the powers, other than powers of appointment, of the governor in council under the Civil Service Act, the Civil Service Superannuation Act, the Defence Services Pension Act, and parts II to VI of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act.
The action taken was not under any of the foregoing acts, nor was it an "appointment". Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act authorizes the governor in council to make regulations with respect to the conditions under which contracts may be entered into, and it was pursuant to these regulations that the contracts were made. Section 5 (2) of the Financial Administration Act has no application whatever to the present situation.
Thereupon Hansard reports that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated the following:
Mr. Speaker, on the question of privilege may I suggest that what I indicated on Friday was that the opinion in the name of Mr. Driedger tabled by the Prime Minister indicated that though it was purported that these arrangements were made under the government contracts regulations in accordance with section 39 of the Financial Administration Act, they do not come within the terms of the government contracts regulations themselves, as Mr. Driedger himself pointed out.
It seems to me that since we have had a question of privilege and a counter question of privilege raised in connection with the subject, the matter should be gone into. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam:
"That sessional paper No. 39B be referred to the committee on privileges and elections for study and report."
At this juncture I suggested that the motion might be allowed to stand until today in order to ensure that there was a prima facie case of privilege involved in the assertions of the two hon. gentlemen.
I do not propose at this time to review the authorities or comment on the nature of parliamentary privilege, but I would refer to the attention of hon. members May's sixteenth edition, pages 42 and 43; Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, page 37 and also Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, beginning at page 93.
The question of the privileges of this house is a wide and complex subject, and to try to cover that subject in a few words could be a most hazardous exercise. However, recognizing the risk that may be incurred in doing so I would say that, stated briefly, a question of privilege is a question relating to the rights, security, dignity and freedom of the house as a whole or of its members individually, and to the conduct and honour of such members.
If my summary of the authorities be substantially sound, I find no support in any of them for the contention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that a prima facie question of privilege of this house is involved in his assertions or in his motion. It seems to me that what we have is, in essence, a dispute between two hon. members with regard to the legality of certain action. In other words I suggest that the matter could be raised as a grievance on a motion to go into committee of supply or at some other appropriate occasion. In this regard may I refer hon. members to paragraph 5 of citation 104 of Beauchesne's fourth edition.
Since there is, in my opinion, no question of privilege involved I cannot give the hon. member's proposed motion precedence over the business set down for today.

Some 5,000 visitors had gathered to see this most interesting attraction on capital hill during the summer months.

speechtext: The guard reached the cenotaph, circled and returned to barracks. It is true that there was a threat of rain, but none was falling and none came. This morning in the opinion of the officer commanding the conditions justified this procedure being carried out, and in consequence the guard did not proceed to parliament hill to carry out the ceremony.

Mr. Chairman, hon. members will recall that there are six separate resolutions on the Customs Act. The first two resolutions relating to that act embody changes in tariff rates and the wording recommended by the tariff board in its last three reports under reference No. 125. In this reference the tariff board was asked to review all the items in the Canadian tariff covering textiles and to recommend a new tariff structure. The final reports, which are now being acted upon, are those covering miscellaneous textiles of jute, hemp, flax and rough fibres, and coated or impregnated fibres, hats, caps and related products. In addition to the changes in tariff and drawback items recommended by the board in the three reports to which I have referred, the resolution contains technical revisions relating to textiles woven of cotton yarns.
Negotiations and consultations relating to the tariff changes proposed in these resolutions were necessary because many of the items in question were bound under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. These negotiations have been completed with all the other countries concerned, specifically with the United States, the United Kingdom, the European economic community, Austria, Yugoslavia, Haiti, India and Japan. The other countries concerned recognized that while certain tariff increases would result from the adoption of the new textile schedule recommended by the board, they would be offset by approximately equally important decreases. As a consequence it was only in respect of rather specific problems relating to Canadian trade with particular countries that Canada was obliged to go outside the textile schedule to find additional compensation.
Hon. members will note that the resolutions contain proposals for reductions of duties on chicory, photographic dry plates, motor scooters, aluminum sluice type irrigation devices, hay stack forms and orchard heaters. These reductions comprise an integral part of the negotiated package. I should add that in this negotiated package a few departures were made from the recommendations made by the board.

I realize that this particular item is often used in conjunction with another item in the Customs Tariff Act. I have forgotten the number but I am sure the minister's officials will know. I understand that over the years the department have developed a ruling of their own with respect to how the word "machinery" should be interpreted. As I recall from conversations with the officials in the past, the word "machinery" is interpreted as having moveable parts. A great many pieces of equipment used for agricultural purposes do not come under this technical interpretation of the word "machinery", and this causes a great deal of inconvenience and over the years has caused a lot of expense and trouble to people in the farm equipment and machinery business, whether retail or wholesale, and I expect at the manufacturing level in some cases.
I was wondering, Mr. Chairman, whether the minister and his officials might give consideration to having that other section redrafted in such a way that this problem
Customs Tariff
would not arise in the future. The problem specifically is that you get some new invention used on the farm which, in the layman's term, is clearly farm machinery yet does not come under the technical term decided upon by the department in interpreting the word "machinery". The result is that the only way the matter can be cleared for non-payment of duty is to get it specifically listed.
There is a long list in front of us now, and there are no doubt more additions and I suppose more will be added over the years. But this could be avoided and much inconvenience avoided as well in the future if the other section which worked in conjunction with this one could be reworded in such a way that the words "agricultural machinery, equipment and the like used on the farm for farming purposes", was used instead of the very narrow term "machinery" which is used at the moment, which necessitates these long lists of specific items being included every time there is a budget. I wonder whether the minister has any observations on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would my hon. friend think it reasonable for me to suggest to the officials concerned that we do take this matter under consideration, and if his suggestion can be implemented that we do it at a later time? If I could just follow that point up, over the years certain items which have been brought across the border, and on which we paid duty, have gradually been added to the list. I see heaters are listed. I believe last year stack heaters were excluded. What the farmer is faced with is the fact that when these pieces of equipment come in he suddenly finds he has to pay duty. This he cannot understand. Therefore if I might lend weight to what the hon. member for Oxford has said, I think there should be an early review of the question with the idea of bringing in some form of farm equipment section which will cover all farm equipment, provided that the equipment is used only as farm equipment.

May I add my observations to those of the hon. member who has just spoken. We have from time to time experienced difficulty with regard to this interpretation of what is and what is not equipment used exclusively for agricultural purposes. associates so we might have a clear interpretation of what is meant by equipment used for agricultural purposes. I wish to refer now to the rockets which are used experimentally to carry silver iodide crystals up into the clouds to induce rain. We acknowledge that these devices are still in the experimental stage, but many farmers in the dry part of Canada are convinced that they do produce results in increasing precipitation when atmospheric conditions are suitable. Would the minister tell us if there are manufacturers in Canada making V-belts?

This is interesting from the point of view that we have been discussing a department of industry and the creation of more jobs in Canada. speechtext: One of the things that I think all hon. members have deplored in the past is the relative shortage of statistics giving a breakdown with regard to manufactured goods in Canada. Mr. Chairman, arising out of the question asked by the hon. member for Lapointe the minister said that as far as he could see there was no revenue significance in the resolution. In regard to resolutions of this sort is there no detailed calculation of how they will affect ways and means in the result?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The best calculation that has been made is that it balances out.

The minister means that it does not affect ways and means at all. Actually my question was whether it is normal practice in the case of resolutions of this kind to make calculations in order to find out how the balance of ways and means is affected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is fair to say, Mr. Chairman, that if the revenue effects are at all significant they are taken into account. In this case the conclusion was that they were not significant. There were some pluses and some minuses, and they balanced out. There is not enough difference to put in your eye.

I should like to say, frankly, that I do not know what the strict procedure is in the discussion of budget resolutions. I noticed that the hon. member for Lapointe, perhaps realizing that these textile items were at the end of the list, used the occasion to make some general remarks. I noticed that the minister did make an opening statement on this resolution. I was wondering, then, if I could be permitted to make some general remarks on this last item? I do not know what the procedural details are in this connection, but we have gone through the item by item discussion, and at the beginning of the discussion I did ask what procedure should be followed. I think there is a certain amount of give and take on these matters and I should like, very briefly, to make a couple of general remarks.
First of all, sir, I should like to mention to the minister and his officials that after examining these items-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do not believe the hon. member would be quite out of order at this stage if he were to keep his remarks rather brief. May I ask him to do that?

At the beginning of the discussion on this resolution, I did ask for some indication as to the proper procedure. Since I have been in the house, it seems to me that every year there is a different procedure followed in the discussion of these budget resolutions. I do not want to be lengthy, and I did not want to open up a general discussion in the middle of the item by item examination, but I do want to make some general remarks on this particular resolution.
My brief remarks are simply these: I am very happy that the minister informed me and the other members of the committee that it is only when significant revenue changes are anticipated that they are reported in so far as they affect ways and means. I think another thing that should be underlined is the fact that as we have gone over the resolution item by item this afternoon, we have become involved with the expression, "of a class or kind made in Canada". During the discussion of one item I did mention the fact, and I should like to repeat it at this stage as we close the debate on the resolution, that this would be a very convenient list to hand over to the new department of industry. I
Customs Tariff
think it is important that we consolidate, as much as possible, the list of a class or kind not made in Canada for future and more profound study.
At this point, I should like to underline the fact that we are passing a resolution which, in principle, goes a long way towards satisfying three things. It would seem that our trading neighbours are satisfied with the results of this package deal which was negotiated, and which the minister took great pains to explain to the house. I thank him for that. It would seem, too, that while no one industry is ever completely satisfied, I think we have gone some distance towards rectifying many of the problems which faced the textile industry. It is more than a mere coincidence that many of the compensatory items involved, and which are inserted in this resolution, will naturally have a beneficial effect upon the farmers of Canada. I should like to point out that this resolution virtually satisfies three such points of consideration.
I should like also to state very briefly, and as uncontentiously as possible, that the administration which I supported for a number of years in this house felt it was very important for Canada to have an operating textile industry, a healthy textile industry. I do not want to be too contentious, but prior to 1957 there was some doubt whether the government of that day thought it was important that Canada should have a textile industry capable of survival. I hope that the presentation of this resolution to the committee indicates that the administration has now come round to the point of view that a healthy Canadian textile industry is something worth while.
The last general point I should like to mention as we close this debate, Mr. Chairman, is the hope that the minister will clarify our thinking on some of these points as the discussion proceeds on the other resolutions to come before us. It would be most helpful if the minister informed us whether the attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the attitude of the Prime Minister is going to prevail in the approach to tariff negotiations in relation to the United States proposal. If the Prime Minister's approach is taken holus-bolus, I think it is right to assume that this attitude will have definite effects on the tariff board's decisions and recommendations. This attitude will have effects on our secondary industries. We would all like to hear about that.
This is all I will say now because if I were to continue in this vein much longer I would no doubt be out of order. I would like to indicate that is the approach we will be

Customs Tariff
having to the discussion of future resolutions. I thought this would be a good time to indicate it. I thank hon. members opposite for their indulgence in allowing me to make these observations at this stage of the discussion. I know there are certain rules covering this discussion, but I thank you for the flexible approach that has been accorded me.

Before the resolution carries, I should like to make a short comment. I know that I have taken up perhaps enough time of the committee this afternoon, but I should like to thank the minister for trying to answer my questions at all times and taking them seriously. Those questions which he could not answer, he has promised to consider. There is one subject, however, with which I have been dealing most of the afternoon, and that is agricultural products.
I know item 409f was dealt with already, but just before we pass the first resolution I would like to point out that it says at the bottom of that item, "all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery not otherwise provided." I asked about four or five particular agricultural products, and in each case was told by the minister that he would have to discuss it with the officials and an individual study of each would have to be made.
Before the resolution passes I wonder could the minister give us some idea regarding what form of a directive is sent to officials in the offices of the Department of National Revenue across the country, with regard to other agricultural implements and machines used in agricultural production. What guidance is given to these officials across the country?
I listed portable livestock scales, steel' boxes with hydraulic dumps, potato boxes, steel potato boxes which are a special machine used on potato farms, potato bagging machines, metal fence stays and a number of other items. Surely the minister could clarify the other agricultural machinery used in the production of agricultural goods? Surely these could be classified under one broad directive and sent to all officials across the country.
I could list a number of cases which I have had the privilege of dealing with, particularly over the last couple of years. I know some of the difficulties that importers and purchasers in Canada encounter in trying to decide whether an imported machine not commonly used in agriculture production, or shall I say specifically used, can come in duty free because it is not specifically listed in item 409f. Further I would point out that under resolution 1 we have three more items added to item 4091

It seems to me that every possible agricultural implement should be listed under this item because, unless they are listed, Department of National Revenue officials across the country tend to turn them down in most cases. The only alternative left to a purchaser is to approach his member of parliament and hope, through his pressure, to get the officials to rescind the tax already paid on an imported machine.
I am sure that if a wide enough directive were sent out to the officials this would not happen, but as it stands at present it is my opinion, and that of a number of people throughout the country, that any item, in order to come in duty free, must be 1'isted under item 4091

Before the minister replies I want to say I listened with a great deal of attention to the hon. member for Acadia when he was questioning the minister on steel boxes for the ordinary farm wagon. The minister said, "Yes, that sounds as though it ought to come in." When an extension was asked on the hydraulic equipment the minister said, "Well now, I think at this stage we should query the actual department, just to make sure whether it comes in or not." It just so happens that a steel box with hydraulic equipment cannot come in duty free. It is not listed.
I am not sure whether the hon. member for Acadia asked about this previously and was turned down, but there is no question about it that such a steel box has a farm use, and has only got a farm use. However, with the hydraulic equipment it is turned down. When the minister was giving his answer on this general category under item 409f, his own common sense told him a farm wagon should come in; but yet he said, "No, I think we had better go to National Revenue and find out whether it should be allowed in or not."
Before the minister answers I would point out that he said steel boxes were duty free. He made this statement, and I think Hansard will bear me out. It certainly bears checking at any rate.

I know, but I think somebody nudged him after he gave the answer. When the hon. member for Acadia started talking about hydraulics, at that stage he began to wonder and I think he got an extra nudge. If the minister feels that common sense says a steel box should come in duty free, then why should not a hydraulic equipped box come in duty free? If the minister is perplexed, then what about the average farmer across Canada, and I am talking about the

western farmer as well as the eastern farmer? Surely they must be really perplexed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I may, I will just clear up this last point. When I was talking about farm wagons we were on item 409f and were talking about gravity discharge farm wagon boxes. This item comes in free, but we all know there are other items in the tariff. Generally speaking-and I suppose it is unwise to generalize in this as in other fields -but by and large agricultural machinery comes in free, and by and large I think it is fair to say that the farmers of Canada know this. I think it is fair to say that most farmers recognize a piece of agricultural equipment when they see it. Then there are borderline cases and there are situations where the case is not clear.
I would point out that the Department of National Revenue has some 47 ports of entry across the country where all the information that is available at headquarters is duplicated and available. If anybody is under any doubt as to whether an item is dutiable or comes in free of duty, all he has to do is ask somebody in one of the offices of the department, or write to the head office. In this resolution-
I wonder-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I finish? We were dealing with fairly certain specific items and I had not undertaken to embark on a full discussion of the tariff, or even on a full discussion of the tariff as it applies to the agricultural industry. I was dealing with these specific items, which for today was about as far as I had hoped I would have to go. I think I will leave it at that.

I want this particular item cleared up before we proceed. The minister stated earlier this afternoon that gravity discharged farm boxes would include wooden and steel boxes, but I think the only type of steel box that would be gravity discharged would be one parked on a hill. The minister made the remark that is often the illusion of many people not directly in contact with the agricultural industry, that an agricultural implement is easily recognizable. Not today it is not. Today agricultural machinery is becoming highly mechanized and farmers are resorting more and more to hydraulic and highly machined equipment. This is, in a sense, part of the automation that has taken place throughout the country in other industries as well as agriculture. When I asked the minister whether steel boxes are included under this item, he said yes. I asked him for the explicit purpose of clarifying that particular thought that was in my mind, and has been in my mind for some time. Now
Customs Tariff
he and the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary are suggesting that steel boxes might be duty free, but if they have a hydraulic hoist attached to them, they are not duty free. Yet further down in item 409f hydraulic hoists are duty free. Perhaps the minister or his officials could clarify the position with regard to this matter. Surely an importer does not have to take the hydraulic hook-up off the steel box and import it separately; surely he should be able to import the two items attached together, if he so desires. This is the point I have been trying to make under this particular item.
It will cost the farmer more money.

As the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary says, it will cost the farmer more money. This is just the point I am trying to make. The government, and we as members of parliament in this house, should try and facilitate the economy of Canada and, in this particular item, the farmers of Canada. We do not want to charge them more money because of an error in the regulations, because of the advanced technological knowledge applied in producing farm equipment today, or because of general automation in agricultural and farm machinery. Surely we should accept the fact that steel boxes with hydraulic hoists attached should come in duty free; that a farmer should not have to send his hired man down to the United States, for example, to take the hoist off the box and let them come in as two items. This is one way he could do it and get around the duty; or if it were cheaper he would pay the duty and keep the hired man at home. This is, in a sense, how ridiculous this item has become. Surely the minister and the officials are prepared now, after our thorough discussion of this particular item, to say that steel boxes with hydraulic hoists are duty free if they are used for agricultural purposes.
I think a purchaser should have to fill out a form and swear that this machine is purchased for agricultural purposes. That is done, in regard to the purchase of machinery, in a number of cases. I can think of air cooled motors, for example; when you buy them for farm use, you fill out a form to this effect, "This machine will be used on the farm for agricultural purposes" and you do not pay the duty. This could also be done in connection with steel boxes with hydraulic hoists attached. I am sure the officials understand that; they are well aware of the forms that farmers fill out and sign. I am sure that if gravity discharge steel boxes can come in duty free, and hydraulic hoists down below can come in duty free, the two items attached should come in duty free. I would like the

Customs Tariff
minister to accept this as a very reasonable argument on behalf of those farmers who are trying to mechanize or further mechanize their farms.

Mr. Chairman, before the item carries I wonder whether I could ask the minister a question for the purpose of bringing those of us who were not here during some of the previous sessions up to date, in line with the point which the hon. member for Acadia suggested has been bothering him for some time. In addition to that there is the fact that previously both these items were included, I think, under tariff item 409f; in other words, they were not added this time. I am wondering whether the representations that are now being made to the minister were made to his predecessor, and what were his reasons for retaining the confusion about which the hon. member has spoken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that thought did occur to me as the hon. member for Acadia was speaking; but I did not want him to think this should influence me to the point where this government would not give his representations the very closest and most careful study. I am sure the officials will do that. We will certainly look into this question.
I do not know that I should answer the question of the hon. member who has just spoken any more than I have, as to why this might not have been dealt with as extensively during the last six years. The hon. member for Acadia looks as though he wants to answer the hon. member himself; he is sort of on the edge of his chair. Perhaps it would be kinder to let him rise and give the answer.

Mr. Chairman, I realize the question was not directed to me but it did implicate me and I would like to say a word further on this item. Perhaps in doing so I can allay the hon. member's anxiety with regard to this particular subject and my actions in connection with it in the last six years.
This matter was brought to my attention about two years ago. I took it up thoroughly and worked hard on it. Then, as I mentioned, because of the vastly changing agricultural scene and the illusion that exists in many people's minds that agricultural implements are easily recognizable, I found it takes some time to convince officials in one government or another that steel boxes with hydraulic hoists that are used on farms should now be duty free. Because government has changed hands gives me no excuse to quit working on this particular item or this particular subject. Perhaps the hon. member for Medicine Hat thinks I should not now continue to press for clarification of this item. But that is not

my understanding as to why I was sent to Ottawa. If a problem existed two years ago, and still exists today, I will continue to work at it and try to have the item cleared up.
Hear, hear.
I was not successful- I should not say "I", because several other hon. members had the same problem-
"We".

We were not successful in convincing the officials that agricultural implements are not easily recognizable. We will continue to work on this subject and I think, thanks to the hon. member for Medicine Hat and his great patience-of course, he was out of the chamber for quite a while this afternoon, so perhaps I did not cause him undue hardship in listening to what I had to say on this particular item-and thanks to his colleagues who have been patient with me while I have been dealing with my agricultural problems this afternoon, I think we have made, with the help of other hon. members, great progress on this very ticklish subject.
The farmers of Medicine Hat will be glad you raised this matter.

I am glad the minister has said he will continue to consider my views and give them serious study. Perhaps because of the arguments advanced this afternoon this whole matter can be cleared up relatively quickly.

Mr. Chairman, this is really on another subject and I am certainly not going to hold myself out as one who is knowledgeable on this matter. I have received inquiries from rural municipalities, from the western and eastern irrigation districts of Alberta in this connection. This is a new subject about which I am completely green and I would ask the minister to explain it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

This item was not included in the resolution. With the help of the officials I could probably give an answer but it might

not be a complete one. In the circumstances I would ask the hon. member to let me get the correct answers and send them along to him. If I try to deal with tariff items at random in this discussion I am afraid we will be here for some time.

question why something was not done under the previous government, and I should like to call this matter, which is very important, to the attention of the minister.
