AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, as I was saying at six o'clock I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee a particular point with reference to items discussed earlier by certain hon. members. The question was asked why action had not been taken under the previous government. I want to make this point very clearly to the minister and his advisers because I think it is most important not only to the house but to Canada as a whole.
I gave an example which admittedly is an old one. I referred to the fact that automatic stock waterers were exempt while automatic stock feeders were not and are not exempt. The real point I should like to make to the minister and his advisers is this, and it is a new one, not an old one. This came about in my constituency only a week or two ago and I think the same thing applies throughout Canada. New industry is developing in Canada and certain items, as in the case of my previous example, are not listed and are subject to duty.
I do not want to leave the impression with you, Mr. Chairman, or with the committee or Canadians as a whole that we are striving to have more and more exemptions made possible for Canadian users. The real point that I think the minister and his advisers should take into consideration is this. I do not think we should have to fight here in committee to have exemptions made for certain articles. I think it should be made known throughout Canada if these articles are manufactured in Canada, and I see no reason in the world that they cannot be or should not be. If they are not available I think they should be made available to Canadians in order to increase secondary production and particularly primary production in the field of agriculture, because whether we like it or not we must admit that across Canada agriculture is one segment of the economy which one might say is in the lower brackets. It is not at the top of the Canadian economy.
Before we move on from this item I want to emphasize, by way of repetition if I have to, the fact that we are not making these arguments just to belabour the government. We are arguing in favour of increasing Canadian production. We are not rehashing old

arguments. As I pointed out earlier, I have a letter here dated as recently as July 11 with respect to a new industry trying to establish itself in my constituency. I do not mean to be selfish by talking about my constituency, and in any event what I am saying applies all across Canada. I referred to the example of stock feeders. I referred to corn coolers, milk coolers and hydro coolers. Hydro coolers are actually only a magnification, if that is the proper word, of these other things. The fact that they are not listed here and apparently are not obtainable in Canada places a very great hardship on a new secondary industry, an industry that Canada needs badly. This is borne out by other speeches we have heard this session.
I should like to leave that thought with the minister. I am not belabouring the point at all. I think they should be made in Canada and perhaps they are available, but as far as this company knows they are not. They are not listed, so the company is hampered in developing a new secondary industry.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped that the minister would tell the committee and the country generally what is included in the words "all other farm machinery" in item 409f. It appears to me and to many others that very little is included in "all other farm machinery". This afternoon I listed a number of types of farm machinery that could come under those words and I thought at one time that the minister was going to give us the directive that the department issues to its officials across the country. Surely that is not asking too much. Surely the minister can make available to us the directive that the department issues to officials across the country in order to clarify once and for all what is included in "all other farm machinery". I listed a number of items this afternoon and I can think of several more. We have been dealing with hemp and woven material. I can think of lariat rope which is used on many farms; but there is a duty on lariat rope coming in from the United States. Certainly that is something used in farming or ranching in southern Alberta and could very well be classified under a broad definition as a piece of farm equipment. Yet a duty is paid on it. Could the minister outline for us what directive the officials receive across the country with regard to this all-inclusive clause in item 409f?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We seem to be back on an item that was dealt with some time ago. This particular item to which the hon. member seems to be objecting is just as it has been for many years. It is designed to allow the importation, free of duty, of all items that
Customs Tariff
are not otherwise provided for. I suppose I can go on repeating the explanation I have given so often, but there is nothing new about this proposal. It has been in the tariff for some time. It is intended to cover all agricultural machinery items that are not otherwise provided for. But, as I say, we have already dealt with this particular item.

I know there was a discussion of this item this afternoon, but the minister has not really dealt with it by way of explanation. He mentions repeating himself, but I have listened very carefully to his remarks and while he has been very kind in enlightening me and the committee on many items, he has not given us an explanation of this matter. I will admit that this item has been in the tariff, but the difficulty I have run into in the last couple of years is trying to ascertain what is included in the phrase "all other agriculture implements". I heard one definition this afternoon to the effect that all agricultural machinery must be on wheels and movable. I took that to be the definition, but I do not believe it is enough. I think it should be wider, and cover a wider range of equipment. It is for this reason I am pressing this argument this evening.
I believe the minister should be able to give the committee an outline of the definition given to officials across the country. No matter in what part of Canada you are, the goods you buy go through the various customs ports such as Calgary, Drumheller or Regina. Nine times out of ten the officials at these places have to make a ruling on a piece of equipment, and surely they have some directives to follow in this regard. All I am asking the minister for this evening is to have his officials give us some idea as to what agricultural implements are included in this item.

Mr. Chairman, this matter was mentioned earlier this afternoon. I think a great deal of the trouble arises, as has been pointed out by many members today, from the restrictive and unrealistic definition of the word "machinery". I am referring to farm machinery. As I understood it, earlier today the minister undertook to review this matter with his officials with a view to redrafting the section. I trust that my understanding is correct.
As the minister pointed out at the time, he would not want to redraft the section on the spur of the moment. I think anyone would agree with that. However, it was my understanding that the minister gave an undertaking that some time in the very near future he and his officials would go over this with

Customs Tariff
a view to redrafting the section, so this problem would not occur as often in the future as it has in the past. In fact we would hope it would not occur at all. Perhaps the minister could tell us whether or not I was mistaken in this understanding.

I do not believe we can say that this particular minister is the one under whom this problem developed. I have always believed that the spirit of the law is important. I think what everyone has missed, particularly the officials, when they were discussing this matter with the minister, was this: What was really intended was that all equipment, whether you call it machinery or equipment, that can produce a dollar on the farm would be exempt from tariff. As the hon. member for Acadia mentioned, we are paying duty on lariats. What I would suggest with the greatest respect is that the wording be changed.
I should like to refer now to the leading case before the privy council in 1936 in which they dealt with the word "banking". I want to draw this analogy. In 1867 we defined the word "banking", and it did not include the lending of money. When the Social Credit government come into power in Alberta they passed certain measures controlling the lending of money. This particular piece of legislation went all the way through the courts to the privy council. Lord Simon said, in that particular decision, that the word "banking" like other words must grow with the economic factors and circumstances of the country. This is what the hon. member for Acadia has been talking about. Basically, the point he has been trying to make with the officials is that farm machinery is not being treated as farm equipment or being defined so that the farmers of western Canada can understand the definition.
This is the problem. We cannot put any blame on the new minister, but I would suggest that his departmental officials think about this and either give us a new interpretation or redraft the section so that the term "farm equipment" encompasses the whole field and includes any equipment that goes to make a dollar on the farm. I do not believe the minister realizes it, but when I raise this question I do so because millions of dollars have been spent and will be spent in irrigating western and southern Alberta. These irrigation companies are really cooperative companies formed by the farmers. They have complained for many years when the old Liberal government was in power, when the Conservative government was in power and now when another Liberal government is in power, that although they use this equipment in farm operations they are

paying a tariff on it. Political science professors have pointed out that when it comes to tariffs, and it is time the country understood this, there is no difference between the philosophy of one party and another in this house. These recommendations are made by the tariff board and if they mean upping the tariff, the Liberal party ups the tariff. They have always painted a picture of themselves as being the low tariff party. They are no more the low tariff party than any other party. We are trying to plan the economy in such a way that it will help all Canadians. I am glad the Secretary of State is here because he spent four or five days last session on this very subject we are discussing now.
Let us get a definition that is workable. This is what all the argument is about. There may be some who feel there is a filibuster going on. There is no filibuster. The farmers want to know where they stand so far as farm machinery is concerned. I have seen articles in the press to the effect that important things come before this house in the dying days of the session, and yet the opposition has remained silent. They allowed these important matters to go through. This is important today to the people of western Canada, and that is why members like the hon. member for Acadia are asking these questions. I do not see the hon. member for Medicine Hat present. He should be questioning this item because he represents a farming community. The farmers of western Canada want a clear-cut definition. That is all they seek. I am coming back to that point when it comes to eastern irrigation equipment. Millions of dollars have been spent and millions of dollars will be spent, and if they are paying tariff on this farm machinery they want to ask the officials why.
Carried.
Before it carries, surely the minister can give some idea or outline of what is included in "other agricultural machinery"?
Mr. Chairman, I think we are out of order. We are now on item 610.
When did you join the Liberal party?
We did the same with you last year. We tried to help you and you did not want it.
We know what help you gave.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. For the enlightenment of the hon. member for Lapointe we are not on item 610. We have passed that item and are on the general resolution No. 1, I should add that it seems to me we are getting

a little far from the principle of that resolution, and I would ask the co-operation of hon. members in limiting their remarks to the resolution.

I appreciate your guidance, Mr. Chairman, but before we close off discussion on resolution No. 1 I think it is important that we arrive at a proper definition regarding agricultural machinery and uses. I am not necessarily asking for an answer tonight, but the minister did make a remark, when I was asking questions under a specific item, that it would only have effect under the excise tax resolutions. It is important we arrive at a good definition of machinery or goods for agricultural use under this resolution, because I am sure all hon. members would agree that by analogy we could easily argue it would have effect on the excise tax resolutions.
I should like to bring to the attention of the committee a typical situation that exists in eastern Canadian agriculture. Very often a piece of machinery that is imported is not specifically designed for agricultural uses. It could be a tractor that might be employed in other commercial uses, but a farmer buys that particular machine because it happens to fit into his particular agricultural operation. He may be a small farmer in Quebec or Ontario -and I am sure the same situation holds true in the west-who often has to use the tractor outside his farm to gain extra revenue.
It is very easy for us in the ivory tower of Ottawa to say that he should get a prior ruling, but he does not get it. Then an inspector comes along and says he is using the machinery principally for non-agricultural purposes. We have gone through this in other parliaments but, as the minister explained so ably an hour or so ago, in practical effect this discussion today would only bear on the excise tax resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The definition may not be perfect but is exactly the same as it was when the hon. member was parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance. I would also like to say I was relieved to hear the hon. member for Bow River say there was no thought on his part of filibustering this particular resolution, and I am sure that is a fact. On the other hand I feel and suspect that some of the questions that have been asked were asked a little earlier this afternoon. Perhaps if we had some new questions it would be easier to deal with them.

Those remarks tempt me to rise once again. The minister said the definition is the same as it was before. I am not saying it is changed; all I am asking is, what is the definition for all other agricultural implements? The item says all other
Customs Tariff
agricultural implements and agricultural machinery. To me the word "implements" is different from the word "machinery." I would call a lariat an implement. It assists a farmer or rancher in his work. I am using this an an explicit example, and I think it should be covered in item 409f.
Some hon. members say we should pass the resolution, but if it is passed now it will not be re-opened until the next budget comes in. I want the definition now, so that we will have the benefit of it for the coming year, and so that we will not have to go into it again next year. We have only one chance to review the budget resolutions and we should avail ourselves of it to make sure we know what changes are proposed.
I think the hon. member for Bow River made a very good point when he brought out the idea that legislation is enacted in the concept of growing. Certainly the term "agricultural implements" or "agricultural machinery" should be considered as a growing term in the legal sense.
We have complained to the department over the last two years that agricultural implements are viewed as though we were still back In the horse and buggy days, but all across Canada we are advancing rapidly out of the horse and buggy days where agricultural machinery is concerned. The minister said the definition is the same as it was before. We want to know what it is and whether it is broad enough to cover the growing aspect of automation in the whole farm machinery picture. Before the resolution passes I hope the minister will give us some outline of the directive that is issued to departmental officials all across Canada.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I wonder why the Minister of Finance will not give the clarification asked for by the hon. members of the opposition.
The minister replied a while ago that the definitions were the same as those figuring in the provisions of the legislation during the last parliament.
Well, what we are asking for is to get some easing or some clarification so that farmers will know what agricultural machinery will be exempt from excise tax and customs duties. Surely it is not when people rise and show arrogance that the discussion can come to an end; this is no way to speed up passage of this budget resolution.
Nowadays, farmers are modernizing their farms. They buy some quite expensive implements and when they go to work outside the farm to get some additional income, they immediately have to pay excise tax and duty on that machinery.

Customs Tariff
We are asking the minister and his officials to set up a catalogue of the implements which must be considered as farm machinery. Is this determined on the basis of manufacturing conditions or of the use made of them?
It is merely in order to get such clarification that we urge the minister to give us an answer. It is surely desirable that he should stop being stubborn and co-operate with opposition members so that we will know where we stand in order to accelerate the passage of this resolution.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to reply to this particular question because I do not think the hon. gentleman was in the chamber this afternoon when I answered this question-
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I must say that I was present in this house this afternoon and I may add that I am perhaps more often in the house than the Minister of Finance, for I am not in the habit of blundering and of slipping away because of my arrogance. I am anxious to do my duty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I recognize the
Minister of Finance.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had no thought of suggesting that the hon. member was not a diligent attender at the sessions of the house. However, I did think that when I answered this particular question he might not have been present. But if he was, perhaps I did not notice him, and I usually do notice him. If he was here, I apologize. If the hon. member was here he will remember that I said in reply to this particular question, put to me by somebody else, that an agricultural implement as such is, under the tariff, an implement that is specifically designed for agricultural use.
Oh, oh.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I finish, please. I daresay there can be some misunderstanding as to what is or what is not specifically designed for agricultural use. But if there is any doubt about it, the doubt can be resolved very quickly by applying for a definition or a ruling from any of the many branches of the Department of National Revenue.

Mr. Chairman, I think the whole point has been missed. I am not trying to be difficult, sir, believe me, but the minister has just said that a machine must be designed for farming, and therein lies the difficulty.

Many machines designed for many things are used in agriculture. I think we should have the wording-this is how I think it should read-to cover all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery which serves farmers and ranchers in their operation of business. This is the point, and I am going to labour it for a moment.
The hon. member for Acadia this afternoon dealt with snow clearing or snow blowing equipment. It may be necessary to have snow clearing equipment to get your products to market. If this equipment is used in agriculture in that regard, it should be free of tariff. The minister says the machinery must be specifically designed for this purpose. I have the greatest respect for the department- and I know they are always behind the minister-but they must grow in the way I stated when dealing with the growing philosophy of that earlier case. The fact is that equipment should be exempt if it is used in agricultural operations of any kind or form. This is what we are trying to make clear. If we could get such a statement from the minister there would be no hold-up of this item as far as I am concerned, and I can almost speak for the other hon. members who represent large farming constituencies throughout Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I have only-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Cariboo.

Mr. Chairman, I am rising to say that in this matter I agree with hon. members who have just resumed their seats, because this is something that not only affects farmers but other people as well. I believe hon. members who have just spoken are right in pursuing this question in order to obtain an answer. I would hope the minister would, in the genial atmosphere of this chamber, rise and tell us that steps will be taken to settle this matter. I hope he will say that anything used in agriculture and which can definitely be shown to be used in agricultural production will be reckoned to be such by the various people he mentioned as being those to whom we could apply for a ruling.
If the minister cannot say now that the ruling will be this or that, when the application is made it is only common sense that the officials are going to say, "It is not of a class or kind that comes under these tariff exemptions" and we will therefore be stuck with this problem. I agree with the hon. gentlemen who have dealt with this matter; I think they are absolutely right.

Mr. Chairman, there is a suggestion I would like to make which might help us out of the difficulty. In view of the restrictive way in which the phrase "farming

machinery" has been interpreted to date, I would hope my suggestion would help solve this problem. I am sure hon. members on both sides of the house have had this difficulty and, as the hon. member for Bow River pointed out, nobody is for a moment suggesting that the Minister of Finance is in any way to blame, because this terminology has been used in the tariff item for years. But it has become an acute problem in the last couple of years, during which time it has been brought to my attention, because of the new types of farm machinery which do not fit into the restrictive interpretation of the word ''machinery".
Naturally one could not expect the minister to redraft the terms of the act on the spur of the moment, because this is a very complex matter. However, I would suggest to the minister that between now and the time the budget bills come down he might discuss the matter with his officials and the Minister of National Revenue and perhaps some way could be found out of this difficulty. Nobody would, of course, expect the minister to make some suggestion now on the spur of the moment, but perhaps he would give an undertaking that he will discuss the matter with his colleague the Minister of National Revenue and his officials, and when the budget bills come before the house some arrangement might have been made.

Mr. Chairman, I fully realize, as do all hon. members, that the Minister of Finance is anxious to balance his budget and therefore he wants every dollar he can get. Perhaps I can suggest something that will throw the odd dollar up his alley. I agree with everything that has been said by my colleagues on this side of the chamber, that every item of farm machinery should be spelled out so that those who import this type of machinery could buy it knowing it to be tariff free.
However, we have the other side of the coin. We should also have a list of machinery which is subject to tariff, which is used for agricultural purposes and which, according to the law, is of a class or kind made in Canada but enters free of tariff. I have one item in mind to which the minister might give consideration. I refer to cabs for tractors and combines, which are made in a factory in Manitoba right in my own constituency, of material better than anything imported from the United States, at a price which meets and beats that of the United States article. Yet these cabs come in tariff free from other countries, and we are up against it in this regard. I suggest that the Minister of Finance should look into this matter. This is one item that is made in Canada by Canadian labour,
Customs Tariff
Canadian brains and with Canadian finance. If anything should receive a little protection, I think this article should, because it is an agricultural implement. These cabs are used on tractors, and our tractors out in the west are used in all kinds of weather conditions. They are mostly used on the farm. It is true that often a farmer will take a tractor out to open up a highway, and he is then accused of not using his tractor for agricultural purposes and the excise boys get right after him. That is not fair, if he has no other way of getting to town, which is often the case. These cabs keep the farmer warm while he is driving the tractor; they shelter him from rain. The same cabs are made for every make of combine. I suggest the Minister of Finance take this under consideration, and it being a product of a class or kind made in Canada it should get the protection it deserves.
I have only one remark which may resolve the problem. The minister is rapidly finishing so he can consult his experts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure that was an ingenuous remark and I will accept it as such. A lot of very useful suggestions have been made in the course of this debate and I can assure all hon. members that they will be taken up and considered very seriously. I think the hon. member for Oxford suggested that it should not be expected that the Minister of Finance should make a snap ruling in these matters, and I thank him for that suggestion. The hon. member for Marquette made a different kind of suggestion, and I was very interested in his exposition of what was being done in his constituency. I will draw it to the attention of my colleague the minister of industry. I think all hon. members will agree that some of these things are not susceptible of being resolved on the floor of the house in a few minutes or even a few hours. All I can do is assure hon. members that everything that has been said will be considered as carefully as it deserves.

I realize the minister will carry out to the letter what he says, but I am not satisfied with the definition he has given the committee. He stated that agricultural implements are specifically designed for agricultural uses, and if so they are allowed in under this all-inclusive item 409f. I want to point out to the minister and his officials that air-cooled motors, whether made by Briggs and Stratton or anyone else, are not designed specifically for agricultural use. I am sure the minister and his officials agree with me when I say that. Yet a farmer can buy them in Canada duty free if he fills out a declaration that they will be used exclusively on his farm for agricultural purposes.

Customs Tariff
An air-cooled motor does not fit the definition the minister just gave us. Why cannot a whole host of other implements used on farms today be handled in the same way as air-cooled motors? To my knowledge there is no reason why a farmer cannot fill out a form and swear that the implement he is purchasing will be used on his farm. The minister says, in effect, that this is the directive issued to the officials, that the machine must be designed specifically for agricultural use.
I was not here when he said that this afternoon, but if I had this matter might have been cleared up a lot earlier. The minister's definition of 409f does not console me at all. If air-cooled motors can be purchased by farmers for agricultural use, duty free, then I submit a whole host of other machines could also qualify. I used as an example a lariat. To me a lariat is designed for catching cattle.
You mean for hanging.
Someone says for hanging. I think a bigger rope is used for hanging. If the hon. member knows anything about ropes he can check with me later.
If the hon. member stays here he will hang himself soon enough.

The Minister of Agriculture, coming from the great city of Calgary, will agree with me that they have been using a lot of lariats recently in that city. A lariat is designed specifically, I think we will agree, for agricultural use.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can I make an offer to the hon. gentleman. I will be glad to pay the duty on any he needs for the next couple of years.
How about the rest of the population of Alberta? Is the hon. member so fat and healthy and so financially wealthy that he can afford them?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would buy two for the hon. member for Bow River.
I want to assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I cannot be bought.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not even with a rope?

Not even with a rope or the offer of a supply of ropes for the next two years. I am not going to be bought that easily. I was sent here by an agricultural constituency basically and many of the items I have mentioned this afternoon have been brought to my attention over the years by my constituents, and I will continue to work for the clarification and the easing of any tariffs which may be imposed upon agricultural implements or implements used for agricultural

purposes. It makes me proud to feel that I have so many cohorts on this side of the house who are working so hard for the reduction of tariffs. I am proud to say that I worked for five years on these items and did succeed in making a number of changes to item 409f. But I did not accomplish everything, and perhaps that was because I had not the assistance of the brains the hon. member for Red Deer has in his party.
I am also proud to say that I did not vote for this budget, which is more than the hon. member for Red Deer can say. He is one of the people who want higher taxes imposed on the Canadian public, whether they be farmers or otherwise. He voted for the 11 per cent tax. I am trying to reduce taxes on agricultural products. I think this is a vital issue to the members sent here by the farmers in agricultural ridings. We are discussing resolution No. 1 which deals with the duty on agricultural implements. This sort of resolution comes up for debate only once a year after a budget, and this is the one time when hon. members have the chance to make changes.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to hear from the minister how he justifies his definition of agricultural implements when air-cooled motors which are not designed specifically for agriculture, but are nevertheless used in a multiplicity of ways throughout Canada, are allowed in. Certainly the same provision should be made for a host of other machinery used for agricultural purposes. I should like to hear the minister explain the definition his department uses in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to say I am very surprised to hear these hon. members speaking so loudly this year on these matters when last year we never heard about them.
You were not around, that is why.

In fact, I think I hear it for the first time. Last year they did not say a word. They had six years in which to do that. What have they done? They never presented a budget last year, yet this year they are crying out loud. Why did they not do this before? They say: "Why don't you join the Liberals?" We have not changed sides. We remain here. Hon. members to my right are the ones who changed. Why? Because last year they stuck to their benches. They never got up.
How do you know? (Translation):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) will agree that as far

as his comments are concerned, he must limit himself to the substance of the resolution that is being discussed.
(Text):

Very well, Mr. Chairman, I think I have made my point. I think they can understand it. If they were mute last year, I hope they will not be blind this year.
We are discussing the problems of the farmers. I know they have problems. In particular, we are discussing the excise tax, not the sales tax. If we try to help the farmers by making unwise reductions in the excise taxes, we might be making trouble for the workers of this country who are ready to build equipment and materials to be sold to our farmers. We have all kinds of industries able to furnish equipment and machinery to our farmers. By abolishing these tariffs we might not help the workers of our country.
(Translation):
The workers of our country who can manufacture that farm machinery will find themselves out of work if an attempt is made to remove the customs duty on all that equipment and that machinery, whether it be snowplows or other material. Our workers would then be deprived of work in our factories, because taxes being higher in Canada than in other countries, prices are higher.
That is why customs tariffs were established, in order to protect Canadian industry. Otherwise, our workers, as well as various other classes of society, would suffer from unemployment, because Canadians would not buy production equipment. Farmers would be the first to be affected, because they would no longer be able to sell their products.

I rise on a point of order. In my opinion, the consideration of this resolution is not an occasion for setting forth a theory on production and consumption. We are considering a particular resolution and I would ask the hon. member for Lapointe to abide by the provisions of standing order 59(2).

I will try to be more to the point than the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere. We are at present discussing a clarification of the Customs Tariff. I am not one of those who would like to increase the tariff to protect industry, but when it is increased inconsiderately, we are asking for retaliation. But there are some reasonable limits to favouring exports without risking retaliation.
I am not an expert, but I believe that those remarks are relevant to the item before us
Customs Tariff
more particularly because of the many exemptions found in the Customs Tariff concerning the importation of many items in our country. This is why, Mr. Chairman, we must assist industry in Canada so that it may produce our farm implements. All sectors of our community, the retailers, the farmers or the labourers must, first of all patronize Canadian production. That way our whole community will benefit, and particularly those who are actively engaged in production, because Canadian products will then be marketed in our country.
We believe industry should be protected not with high tariff walls but with normal tariff. Mr. Chairman, we do not object and let us not be accused of being Liberals, as was mentioned a moment ago, because in connection with the 11 per cent tax on building materials I did not hesitate to protest as I will do again if need be. When the time comes I will again enter the debate because we do not talk for the pleasure of hearing our own voices. When there are improvements to be adopted, we must set aside all partisan and political considerations, which is not what the Conservatives have been doing for the last few hours.
I would like to conclude by saying this: I am very happy to see that the Minister of Finance, while introducing this resolution, has not deemed necessary-and had he done so we would have blamed him for it-to impose a tariff surcharge that would have been more prejudicial to this country than the present problems.
(Text):

I should like to say a few words after that verbose speech. The hon. member made some strong remarks directed, I suppose, against myself and other members who have been fighting hard to make a case on behalf of farmers all across Canada so that the items they need, the implements they use, might be available to them at a cheaper cost so that they in turn produce more cheaply. He suggested that I had been very quiet in the recent years. Let him check back in Hansard at any time; I wager I made just as many speeches last session as he did.
Not as intelligent, though.

I will let the public judge as to their relative intelligence. In any case I am pleased to see exactly where the Social Credit party stands with regard to the question of lower tariffs on farm machinery. Apparently they are opposed to this idea-I gather so from the remarks just made by the hon. member. That party has three spokesmen

Customs Tariff
now, the hon. member for Lapointe, the hon. member for Red Deer, and the other more notorious hon. member who they are trying to
get rid of. They really should not worry about him because I am sure when they do get rid of him the hon. member from Lapointe can fill his boots without much trouble.
I wish to deal with resolution No. 1 which includes this first item 409f, which the minister has suggested the committee should adopt. Perhaps, after study, we should adopt it. I am sure I will be satisfied if the minister would inform the committee and myself how air-cooled motors are brought in under the definition he gave us a while ago-that of implements used for agricultural purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. member like me to give him his answer right now?
Fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The motors he is referring to come into Canada duty free under 409q.

Thanks. I do not have 409q in front of me but I am accepting what the minister says. I intend to pursue this matter a little further, if hon. members will bear with me. I would not want to think the Liberal backbenchers were trying to suppress free speech by interrupting what I have to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member kindly resume his seat. I should like to remind the hon. member again that in the course of his speech he should try to limit his comments and remarks to the resolution before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I would be pleased to limit my remarks to resolution No. 1. I must admit I was sidetracked by some comments thrown at me and I apologize for more or less allowing myself to be baited. I will deal with resolution No. 1. The minister stated that aircooled motors are brought in under item 409a.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Item 409q.
Well, I was close.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, if I could have your attention for a moment I should like to deal with what the minister said. He suggested that air-cooled motors to be used for agricultural purposes come into Canada under item 409q and are exempt. Fine. All I am saying is that all the other implements that I and other members have suggested should also come in under one item or another and be exempt. We only

have a certain number of items before us and that is why I am dealing with the items that are before us.
I should like the minister to comment on this proposition, and it does not necessarily mean a change in these items. However, before resolution No. 1 passes I should like to hear the minister comment on this suggestion with regard to the wording: "All other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery which serve farmers and ranchers in their operations, not otherwise provided". Surely it could be made clear with those two or three or six additional words. It could even be shortened. You could say: "All other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery used in agricultural production". Maybe those three or four additional words would solve the situation and give a clearer understanding to the officials all across the country and a clearer and more precise understanding to all people wishing to buy machinery for use in the development of their farms, something that we very much want to see them do. The farmers have been in a cost-price squeeze over the years and we have all been trying our best to help them to meet rising costs.
I do not want to be a party to any group which suggests that we should not lower tariffs. I think the principle was initiated a good many years ago that farm machinery, whether it comes from England, Ireland or anywhere else in the world, should enter Canada duty free.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: By Mackenzie King.

The tariffs have been reduced gradually since 1897 by various governments, and I think the record will prove that is so. Certainly I read in the Gordon economic report that the Conservatives removed just as many tariffs as the Liberals did. If hon. members want to check that, it is in the Gordon royal commission report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What page?

I can give you the page. If you will bear with me a minute I will look it up. I think the principle has long been accepted in Canadian agriculture and in the Canadian parliament that agricultural machinery should come into Canada duty free. Certainly farmers today are purchasing tractors and combines. These are the big items in farming today on which the farmers spend their money. Nearly 50 per cent of the money spent by farmers on agricultural machinery is spent for the purchase of tractors. They are duty free, but here we are quibbling about smaller accessories. If large machinery is

allowed to enter duty free certainly the principle should be well established that accessories should also enter duty free whether they be lariat ropes, a snowplow or a piece of fence
Or a calf.

-or steel boxes, or what have you. The principle is an accepted one in the Canadian parliament since away back in 1897, and the tariff was gradually reduced from that time onward. Surely, therefore, we should accept the idea put forward this afternoon that the definition should read "all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery which serve farmers and ranchers in their operations". Surely that would not be straying from the principle or bringing any new concept into the legislation. Certainly not. There is no straying from the principle, no straying from the concept or intent of the original legislation. It would be no trouble at all to add three or four words to that particular clause.
I do not really think it has to be done by way of amendment tonight, as long as we have the assurance of the minister that the department will issue a directive to officials all across the country so that from now on all machinery used on farms for agricultural production will enter Canada duty free, and so that all the farmer will have to do if duty is charged is to sign a declaration similar to that used in the case of air-cooled motors. All the minister has to do is accept the principle that all farm machinery should come in duty free.
As far as the government is concerned there is no particular amount of money involved here. The government is budgeting for a deficit of nearly $800 million, but there is no great amount of money involved here as far as they are concerned. There is a great deal of money involved, however, in the case of the farmer who is trying to automate by adding to his machinery and thus perhaps lowering his expenses. He may buy a machine to take the place of a labourer or something like that. But certainly there is no deviation from the principle in the argument I am trying to present. There is no deviation from the original concept, and I can see no harm in the minister saying that this resolution will now be interpreted to mean that it includes all machinery for agricultural purposes. I should like to hear the minister comment on my suggestion with regard to the issuing of directives to officials across the country on the ruling respecting all agricultural implements.

Before the minister replies may I say that I am sure the minister perhaps does not appreciate just how serious this
Customs Tariff
matter is. Some of us who have been in the house for some years have followed the principle he laid down this afternoon of making representations to the department and accepting rulings on various types of machinery with regard to which we had requested a ruling. In nearly every instance, unless it was covered specifically in the regulations, the rulings went against the persons applying for exemptions from duty under the act.
I think that perhaps one of the basic reasons for this is the fact that agriculture is progressing much faster than the regulations covering it. In various areas of Canada today tremendous amounts of money are being invested in machinery used for agricultural purposes. One reason I cannot accept the minister's definition tonight with regard to agricultural implements and agricultural machinery arises from the fact that there are instances now where air conditioning is being used for livestock buildings, and by no stretch of the imagination can anyone say that air conditioning was designed specifically for agriculture.
We are very much concerned about this matter not only because there are a great many implements involved but because some of the implements are extremely costly and the imposition of a tax makes quite a bit of difference in the cost price to the farmer. We are also concerned about the great number of new implements coming on the market each year which are designed specifically to advance the automation of agriculture. These are the things we are vitally concerned about and this is why we feel some help should be provided. I believe that the minister was sincere and earnest in his presentation this afternoon, but as far as we can gather there is no intimation that the procedure to be followed will be any different from that followed in the past. This, sir, is not good enough for the farmer of today. He wants to know when and how he can get the necessary relief that we feel is so desirable at this time.
Mr. Chairman, since this question is of great interest to the farmers of this country, we would appreciate very much hearing the views of the Minister of Agriculture on this matter.

I dislike taking up the time of the committee at this moment, but there are several hon. members who have made a reference, indirectly, to the Canadian people, and I do not believe it should be allowed. As a matter of fact, there was a reference directly to hon. members beside me in another party. The hon. member even went so far as to say, "Where have you been

for the last two years?" I might ask him the same question, and I am referring to the hon. member for Lapointe.
Order.

speechtext: Order, would the hon. member resume his seat? When remarks along this line were made by an hon. member a moment ago I called him to order and I am doing the same thing in these circumstances.

I thank you, Mr. Chairman. I should like to remind you, and other hon. members of the house, of what has been said in this committee. As a matter of fact, we were talking about the development of Canadian industry. We were not criticizing for a moment. Actually, we were asking the minister, or calling his attention to the need for the development of Canadian secondary industry. Earlier, Mr. Chairman, I quoted from a letter dated July 11 from one of my constituents. It is not dated two years ago, but is dated 1963. I think other hon. members of this house might do well if they read their mail, and they might find one of these letters from their own constituents.
I am going to be brief, Mr. Chairman.
Oh, oh.
I still think the minister could get around this difficulty, and I say this with sincerity-
Can we believe you?

It is all right for you people, but somebody has to be concerned with the farmers, and we certainly happen to be concerned about them.
While I am answering, and in spite of the fact you brought several members to order tonight, Mr. Chairman, I want to answer the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He said that it was the government of Mackenzie King that set down the terms of reference when farm machinery came into this country free of duty. Let him come forward tonight with the evidence that farm machinery coming into this country was at any time subject to a tariff, either under a Conservative or a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will accept that challenge right now. The duty which previously was on farm implements was taken off completely in the budget of 1945.
Not all machinery.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can find that out very easily by looking up the budget speech, which perhaps would be a profitable exercise.
I said all machinery.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I said farm machinery.

I said all farm machinery, and that is my answer to you.
I want to go back to what I was saying before I was sidetracked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I still say that this problem could be solved if we could have an assurance from the minister that all agricultural implements or agricultural machinery which serves farmers or ranchers in their production, would be free from tariffs. We have heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has expounded on the idea to get rid of tariffs. They are supposed to be the tariff free party. Let us have some evidence of what they have been preaching since the days of confederation.
Let us have the evidence.

We are asking for only one thing, that you assure the farmers that whatever equipment they use for production will be free from tariffs. Surely, that is not too much to ask from the Minister of Finance or his department tonight.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Acadia has roamed everywhere from lariats to snow blowers during this discussion. I do not think it is inappropriate that he should be concerned with blowers. It certainly should be a matter of vital concern to him. He also professes to speak in this house on behalf of all the farmers of Canada. It may be that he speaks on behalf of the poor, downtrodden impecunious wheat farmers, but I think there are other farmers in Canada. I think, in that regard, the hon. member for Lapointe stood head and shoulders above the hon. member for Acadia when he made his statement.
The farmers I represent-and I represent some too-are quite willing to have some reasonable concession in the tariff such as we have at present whereby the farming community and the industrial community can live in harmony. This enables the industrial workers to have money with which to buy farm produce. I think all this item attempts to do, when it comes to giving protection, is to put a tariff on those items which are produced in Canada, so that the Canadian manufacturer-
It does no such thing.

If this is not the case, Mr. Chairman, then the seatmate of the hon.

member for Acadia is off on a different tangent. This is the trouble with the party across the way: The left hand never knows what the right hand is doing. The hon. member's seatmate has just finished requesting protection for his industry at home, which is exactly the kind of thing this item attempts to do. It attempts to give some freedom from tax on machinery, but at the same time give protection to those items which are made in Canada, I think this is what the measure does. I think this is what most of the farmers in Canada want, irrespective of what the hon. member for Acadia may believe his constituents want.

I had no intention of speaking again on this item, but the hon. member for Renfrew South tempts me to do so, as does the silence of the minister. The hon. member said that resolution No. 1 exempts from duty those items not manufactured in Canada and puts a tariff on those items manufactured in Canada. Well, Mr. Chairman, if members did a little homework or at least paid some attention to what is said in this committee, they would surely know that Cockshutt tractors were at one time made in Canada, and may still be made in Canada. Well, tractors have come into Canada duty free for many years. How does that apply to this item?
It doesn't.

Certainly not, it does not. Item 409f of resolution No. 1 deals with items which shall be exempt from tax, and it includes three additional items specifically, aluminum sluice type devices for controlling water in irrigation ditches, haystack forms and heaters for orchards. Those are the only three items that it includes specifically. This is the reason the whole debate has been engendered. We want all agricultural implements, and all implements used for agricultural purposes, allowed in duty free; and as I pointed out the major, big and costly items now used in agricultural production do come in duty free. I am sure the minister will agree with that concept, and that his party will, even though it may have many members who want protection. They have retreated from one position to another and now they may well be termed accurately the high tariff party of Canada.
In rising to speak on this item I certainly feel I represent my constituency, but I also realize that in coming to this great place one must speak for those things which are beneficial to all Canada. I have tried to make my remarks general enough to include the east and the west. I do not want to belong to a party that wishes to split Canada between east and west, as the party opposite now does 28902-5-145

in agricultural matters. I do not want to become a part of that thought. I want Canada united. I want farmers in eastern Canada to enjoy the same privileges as farmers in western Canada.
I want farmers to be able to get their implements in duty free. This is a principle that has been established over the years. As matters stand now, if a farmer is a particularly good arguer and is sufficiently cantankerous, whether he be in New Brunswick, Renfrew, Calgary or Drumheller, he can convince a departmental official that what he is importing qualifies as an agricultural implement and he can have the 20 per cent tariff taken off.
This matter should be explicitly nailed down this evening, particularly since we have spent so much time on it, and since so many hon. members have shown such a great deal of interest in it. We should at least accomplish something this evening for the benefit of farmers all across Canada.
Carried.

I know that many hon. members do not care about farm problems. They want to see this carried and they think these matters are not important. I know there are people in Canada who do not care a hoot about the farmers; but the farmers are the backbone of the nation and of the economy of the country, and will remain so for a good many years. Members of the Social Credit party wish to put this through in a hurry, but we can solve this sticky problem this evening if the minister will give an assurance he will discuss the matter with his officials and ensure that the words in item 409f will include all machinery used for agricultural purposes, or used for the production of agricultural goods.
Air conditioners?

I hear a chorus of nonsense coming from the other side of the house. Certainly if radios help to produce more milk, then they are agricultural implements. The hon. member for Renfrew South owns a dairy farm. It is a great dairy country down there, and they grow a little tobacco once in a while if the Liberal party does not outlaw it. I think Webster would agree with me when I say a proper definition of the word "implement" is a tool used to assist somebody in his work. I am sure some highly trained legal advisers would agree with that definition. It is a tool in this case used to assist farmers, and this afternoon the hon. member for Lethbridge suggested that automatic feeders should also qualify. Certainly they are a tool used to assist in the

Customs Tariff
feeding of beef cattle, and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture would agree with that.
So far we have had nothing but silence or nonsensical quips from backbenchers on the other side with regard to the suggestion I have tried to make within the last hour.
Why not within the last five years?

Surely some of the backbenchers opposite represent farmers in eastern Canada? I know there are not many of them represent farmers in western Canada, but those who do represent farmers must know this is important and should bring pressure to bear on the minister and his officials. We should have this definition made clear once and for all.
I do not want to propose an amendment to this tariff item. I do not want to go into that detail. All I am asking is that the minister issue a directive to the officials all across Canada that from now on machinery used in the production of agricultural goods shall come into Canada duty free. This is nothing new. It is a well established principle and a concept that was agreed upon by parliaments years ago.
I am taking this opportunity to express my views and thoughts on the matter. Some hon. members say this should have been done earlier. I agree wholeheartedly with them; but because it was not accomplished earlier, I am trying to accomplish it now. It is not a question of getting re-elected or not. It is a question of coming down here and doing a job.
As I said before, I represent a constituency largely devoted to agricultural production. You might well term me an agricultural representative, and I see no harm whatsoever in arguing on behalf of the farmers, even though some hon. members would like this item to pass hurriedly. I sat quite patiently this afternoon while the committee dealt with textiles. There are no textiles produced in my constituency.
All I am asking now is that the minister accept the principle which was established years ago that all agricultural implements should come into Canada duty free. The concept has been proven in law that the interpretation of legislation must grow with the economy. This definition of agricultural implements has not grown as it should have in the past number of years.

members do not have to hear the same sentence repeated more than ten times during the same day.

If I have to repeat it a number of times for the particular hon. member, in order for it to sink in, I guess I am prepared to do so. If he is not interested in agriculture, fine. Now?

I am not asking for the impossible. I am not asking that the resolution be changed. All I am asking is that the definition and the directive sent out to officials across the country be broadened and widened to take in the whole scope of this now vastly automated agricultural economy in which we are living. Certainly that is not too much. Certainly we as legislators cannot continue to allow the existence of this problem which so vitally affects our primary industry and the life of our farmers. We cannot continue to view it as though we were still in the horse and buggy days. We must advance our views on this important subject. We must bring our views up to date if we are to be effective, if we are to bring about legislation which will accomplish the aims of the legislators.
This is all I am asking this evening, to raise our sights; to have a new fresh look at the agricultural industry as it exists in Canada today; to bring our views and opinions up to date on what this industry needs and what it is doing. Certainly if we are to bring about legislation which is accurate and effective, and if we are to bring about proper changes in item 409f, we should apply our minds to this problem. It has been the complaint with regard to this item that unless an item is specifically listed here you have to pay duty on it. I do not think it is possible to list all the agricultural implements or agricultural machinery used for agricultural purposes, because these implements, machinery and the agricultural economy are continually changing. What is not used in farming today may be used in farming tomorrow. That is why I am opposed to the idea of three items being added to this resolution today. I am opposed to it because three is not enough; you must add a whole host. I do not think we could possibly add enough. We must, with regard to this all-inclusive clause at the

bottom, "All other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery'', take it to mean precisely what it says. "All other" is what it says, and we must take it to mean precisely that. If the minister would rise and say yes, that is what it means, I would quickly sit down-
Hear, hear.

-and for my part this item could pass. If the minister would rise and say yes, the all-inclusive clause includes all other agricultural implements and machinery. I would be satisfied. But certainly we should not lose this opportunity of presenting our views, of strongly arguing the case for farmers all across Canada that tariffs in connection with agricultural machinery and implements should be reduced.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, the section already reads, "All other agricultural implements". My hon. friend might read the section; that is what it says.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak to the point of order. The hon. member seems to have missed the point. We are not complaining of the use of these words in the section; it is the interpretation applied to them to which we object. Certainly equipment used on the farm or used in the production of agricultural products has not been free of tariff, and unfortunately some of these producers have to quibble and argue with the department. Sometimes they win; sometimes they lose. That is the point the hon. member for Acadia and other hon. members have been trying to make this afternoon. The hon. member raises a point of order, but I say this discussion is in order; what the hon. member is discussing and wants clarification on is the law as applied to this item.
That is exactly the point.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether the hon. member for Acadia would permit a question, then.
Certainly.

The hon. member has referred to the words "all others", which are already in the section. One of his associates on the other side of the house has said he wants, I take it, air conditioning equipment included. I wonder whether the hon. member for Acadia would include air conditioning.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit me to ask him a question?
Yes.
Yes, as long as it is an intelligent one.
Suppose some farmers live on an island and have to have a yacht to go across to their island; would the hon. member include the yacht under this item?
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to comment on the "ifs" and "ands" of what I would do, and so on and so forth. I am being sidetracked by these comments.
Oh, oh.
I was in the position where I was going to say something.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

The hon. member addresses all his questions to the minister. Supposing the minister does not know, or has no knowledge of agricultural implements? Perhaps the hon. member should address his questions to the officials here.
Or the Minister of Agriculture.
Or the Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I have been trying to make my remarks general, and on two or three occasions this afternoon I asked the Minister of National Revenue particular questions. Earlier this evening I asked the Minister of Agriculture for assurance with regard to several items which I mentioned, and I took his silence to mean he was in agreement with me; and I am sure he was, on those particular items. To get back to the subject and the point I am trying to make-
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

I have sat for 4| hours now listening to this interesting discussion. I wondered whether the hon. member could give us some kind of economic reason why

Customs Tariff
the farming community should be singled out for this special type of concession against any other section of the economy. I am perhaps giving him additional leeway to get going again, but I would be interested in hearing from him some purely economic reason for granting these particular concessions to the farmers as against any other part of the industrial community of Canada.
Well, I am not going to be sidetracked by this question.
Oh, oh.

Oh, I would love to deal with it. Certainly we all know the conditions which existed throughout Canada and the position the farmers were in. The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have just been out to western Canada, where they saw a wonderful crop in the growing stage. But who knows whether at this very moment tonight hail might not wipe it all out. A year ago the air force had to fly grasshopper poison to the aid of farmers in western Canada. Farming is a very risky operation and livelihood. A crop is never harvested until it is in the bins and even then it may spoil. Farmers have no unemployment insurance or many of the other insurances of other classes of business. All one need do is look at the income figures to see how farmers eke out a living providing for their families as best they can. Perhaps the hon. member was serious in his question, but this is the first time I have ever known a New Democratic party member support higher tariffs on agricultural machinery. I am sure the former premier of Saskatchewan knows full well the hazards farmers face from day to day and from year to year.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of privilege; I was not suggesting we were dealing with the tariff one way or the other. What I was asking the hon. gentleman, and obviously he is not the slightest bit interested in responding, was to give us a logical, economic reason, instead of a lot of hollering and shouting such as we have listened to over the last four and a half hours.

I am sorry if I appear to be hollering and shouting. I tried to answer the hon. member's question but I do have to contend with a continual and nonsensical yapping, and I have found that if I raise my voice I drive my point home a little more quickly. I want to sit down. I am tired of pressing this argument. One has only to look at the figures to see the incomes of the farmers throughout Canada. I am arguing the principle which has been accepted by parliament in years gone by. It is a well established

principle and I do not want to go back and rehash it. I am asking the minister and his department to accept this concept wholeheartedly and to interpret the word "implement" as I think it should be interpreted.
Explain.

Now they want a definition of the word "implement". My definition, which I am sure will be supported by Webster, is that it is anything used as a tool for the aid or assistance of the person using it.
Oh, oh.

They can laugh. Perhaps some of them have mowed their lawns recently. Well, a lawnmower is an implement, but not necessarily an agricultural implement. Perhaps they have actually hoed a garden. In this case the hoe would be an implement but not necessarily an agricultural implement. If one turns on a sprinkler, then the garden hose to which it is attached would be an implement. It is assisting in the spreading of water on a lawn, but it is not necessarily an agricultural implement.
What about a rake?

The minister and his officials will agree deep down that this is a realistic and a proper view of the word. The hon. member for Renfrew South, if he were minister, would apparently agree that the broad concept of agricultural implements should be accepted, and I think the minister should stand up and say: "Yes, this is my interpretation and I will so direct the officials throughout Canada". That is all I am waiting on.
If the minister will be kind enough to do that we can pass on to other items, and I only wish his backbenchers would give him the opportunity to stand up before they immediately holler "Carried".
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Acadia was unable to give the committee the reasons for his argument I should like to do so on behalf of this group. I think his argument is soundly based. If an examination were made of the bureau of statistics figures the return per thousand dollars invested in Canada in agriculture compared with the return per thousand dollars invested in industry can be ascertained. Reference was made to yachts in a rather playful manner, and I understand farm transportation is exempt from duty. Would the minister include as an agricultural implement a launch required by a farmer who had no other means of transportation but water?

Mr. Chairman, this resolution provides for a miscellaneous group of amendments, mostly of a relieving nature, affecting 22 different tariff items. As hon. members may have noted, the effect of several of the proposed amendments is to enlarge the scope of existing free entry items by adding the words which are shown in italics. It is also proposed that several items which provide for the free entry of specified goods for limited periods of time, for example, heavy water, borate ore for use in fighting forest fires and aircraft of types and sizes not made in Canada, be extended for further periods.
Item 703b deals with the tourist exemption and I might make special reference to it. The proposed amendment to 703b would provide statutory authority for a reduction in the tourist exemption. That is the amount which returning Canadians may bring in duty free and which has already been in effect for more than a year. It was introduced by order in council P.C. 1962-903 of June 24, 1962.
No doubt many Canadian travellers to the United States and other countries woud be glad to make use of larger exemptions if they were available. However, experience shows that this change is making a substantial and relatively painless contribution to improving our balance of payments on travel account.
Since 1936 tariff item 703b has provided that Canadian residents returning from abroad after an absence of 48 hours may bring in with them free of duty goods to the value of $100 provided four months have elapsed since their last claim. In 1958 provision was made that in addition to the $100 basic exemption a resident returning from overseas after an absence of not less than 14 days might claim an additional exemption of $200. If advantage is taken of the special exemption no further exemption, basic or special, may be claimed for a further 12 months.
The statutory provision relating to the tourist clause has not been amended since 1958. However, P.C. 1962-903 of the 24th of June, 1962 had the effect of reducing the basic exemption to $25 and the special exemption to $75. The limitation is having a substantial effect on imports. In the six months July to December, 1962, total imports under item 703b were only $19.6 million compared with some $43 million in the corresponding months of 1961. Imports from the United States dropped from $35.6 million to $12.9 million for the period. In the peak year of 1960 total imports under the item were $82 million of which $71 million were from the United States.

Customs Tariff
Taking account of undeclared imports and expenditures for accommodation, the total net saving in our tourist account with the United States attributable to the change in the exemption is likely to be of the order of $70 million to $80 million per annum. Other factors, including changes in exchange rates, are also contributing to an improvement in the over-all balance of our travel account. We had a deficit on travel account in every year from 1953 to 1962 inclusive. The deficit reached a peak of over $200 million in each of the years 1959 and 1960. It declined to $160 million in 1961 and $50 million in 1962. In 1963 we are likely at least to break even and may well have a surplus.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to see statutory provision being made for the changes in the tourist exemptions. This is part of a program encouraged by the former administration to take the greatest advantage of the tourist industry. For a long time there was a failure to appreciate the economic significance of this important industry. I know my hon. friend the Minister of National
Customs Tariff
Revenue has always taken a keen interest in this subject but there is still some scepticism concerning the importance to the Canadian economy of this industry, particularly in relation to its impact on the exchange situation. I wonder whether the minister has any projections as to the possible impact this will have on the exchange situation in the ensuing year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member was not in the house when I gave this information in introducing this resolution. I included a fair amount of detail. If he would like me to repeat it I will but he will find it all in Hansard.
If the minister gave these projected figures I will see them in Hansard tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did give them in some detail.

With regard to the balance of payments position, is the minister not thinking primarily of the United States in connection with these items? I believe the influence of imports from Japan and Germany has had an effect with regard to price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I referred to the effect on the balance of payments, and our major problem here is with the United States. The big item in the tourist expenditures would be with the United States, although the tourist expenditures in other countries would have some bearing.

Would it not be true that imports of a good many things tourists buy in the United States can now be obtained at lower cost, shall we say, from other places as well, and these imports would affect this matter as much as the $25 limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so. I think the expenditures which tourists made a few years ago primarily in the United States were substantial. They are not spending their money in the United States to the same extent now. They are spending it in Canada or saving it, I do not know which. To the extent they are spending it in Canada, most of it would be spent, I would suspect, on Canadian manufactured goods, although some would be spent on imported goods too.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Resolution agreed to.
Resolutions 5 to 6 agreed to.

speechtext:
We will now consider the resolution respecting the customs tariff surcharge on imports order.
Resolved,-That it is expedient to introduce a measure in the following terms:
1. The order of His Excellency the governor in council of the 24th day of June, 1962, expressed to

Customs Tariff
be made pursuant to subsection (1) of section 4 of the Customs Tariff and pursuant to section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, shall be deemed for all purposes to have had the same force and effect as if it had been validly made on that day pursuant to an act of the parliament of Canada that authorized the making of that order.
2. All rates of customs duties more favourable than those of the general tariff, and the benefit of any tariff more favourable than the general tariff, expressed to be withdrawn by the order mentioned in section 1, shall be deemed to have been restored on the 1st day of April, 1963, and from and after the 1st day of April, 1963 the rates so restored and any tariff the benefit of which is so restored shall, subject to the provisions of the Customs Tariff, apply as they applied immediately before the 25th day of June, 1962.

speakerposition: topic
Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have made very good progress today and I should like to express appreciation to all hon. members for their co-operation, as well as to certain hon. members in particular for some of the most fervent and extraordinary oratory we have heard in this chamber for a long time.
With respect to the bill we have just finished discussing, I think it would be better to leave it, now, until Friday because, notwithstanding what I announced last night, we would like, tomorrow-and I have spoken to the representatives of the parties opposite about this-to go back to the economic council bill and see if we cannot complete it tomorrow afternoon. This would mean a good deal of progress toward the goal which I think we all have in mind. Then we would come back and start afresh on the budget resolutions on Friday, with the resolution on the income tax. On Thursday, of course, we take the resolution on the Canada pension plan bill.

Can the leader of the house give us any indication of the order in which we shall deal with the other budget resolutions? I am thinking of the sales tax, for example. I have in mind the convenience of other hon. members. I am not speaking for myself.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Subject to consultation with hon. members opposite we would perhaps take a few minutes at the beginning of our time on Friday to finish off the Customs Tariff, if I hear from hon. gentlemen that it
[The Chairman.]

is really a formality. This would give us something to send to the other place. Then we would go on with the income tax resolution on Monday, if we did not finish it on Friday, until it was completed. Immediately thereafter we would take the excise tax or the sales tax-it is the same thing-until it was completed. Then there are, of course, the bills which follow these two.

Can the Secretary of State tell us why it should be desired to begin the resolution on pensions before the federal-provincial conference has met? I think that matter should be dealt with only after that conference has been held.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman referring to the Canadian pension plan?

Yes.
Business of the House Mr. Pickersgill: There is no thought of proceeding with that measure beyond the stage where hon. members would have had an opportunity to debate the general scheme which the government has in mind. The purpose of this, as outlined in the Prime Minister's letter to the premiers, was to make the scheme public so that there would be something to discuss at the conference. It is precisely so that we would not be in contempt of parliament that we wish to bring this forward at the present time. It would not be proceeded with. It would just be exposed here and hon. members would have an opportunity to say something about it. It would then be available for the conference to discuss.
